content.headline: Riyadh airport attack kills 12 as Saudi coalition vows response
content.shortHeadline: 12 killed in attack on Riyadh airport
content.standfirst: More than 300 people were injured and flights suspended after the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in years. The Saudi-led coalition blamed the Houthis, who have not claimed responsibility for Saturday’s strike.

image.caption: Smoke and flames rise at King Khalid International Airport after the attack.

sources.originalTitle: Twelve killed in attack on airport in Saudi capital Riyadh
Twelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airport
Mindst 12 personer dræbt efter tredje angreb på lufthavn i Saudi-Arabien på en uge

segments.body: At least 12 people were killed and 309 injured when an attack hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi authorities said. The dead included citizens of Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt. Airport operations were suspended as damage was assessed.

segments.title: A wider escalation
segments.body: The Saudi-led coalition blamed the Houthis and called the attack a war crime, pledging a response. The Houthis have claimed responsibility for earlier strikes on Saudi airports this week but had not taken responsibility for Saturday’s attack. The UN’s Yemen envoy warned of a grave escalation and a threat to regional security; Donald Trump said the US would consider joining Saudi strikes.

perspectives.body: The Danish embassy in Riyadh described Saudi Arabia’s security situation as unstable and unpredictable, and warned that airports, including Riyadh, could remain targets. Several airlines cancelled flights and Western embassies advised citizens to stay away.

content.headline: Trump calls for Zelenskyy’s removal after US-Russia diesel deal
content.shortHeadline: Trump calls for Zelenskyy’s removal after diesel deal
content.standfirst: A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia killed at least 20 people, including children, as Trump defended a deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. Ukraine says the agreement gives Moscow revenue to prolong its war.

image.caption: Rescuers evacuate a wounded woman from a building struck in Zaporizhzhia.

sources.originalTitle: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 20 people
Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia
'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
Ukraine war briefing: Trump and Zelenskyy’s public tussle over Russian fuel deal worsens
How Ukraine’s latest attack could shape the war – and Trump’s support
Trump’s Putin deal is a desperate attempt to win voters – Ukraine will pay for it
USA-Korrespondent efter Trumps opfordring til ukrainsk præsidentskift: Fredsbestræbelser har det svært
Analytiker: Amerikansk dieselaftale med Rusland er et plaster på såret, men det løser intet
Rusland muliggør dieseleksport til USA ved at fjerne eksportforbud
Trump køber diesel af Putin, og det huer ikke Zelenskyj: Giver Rusland penge at føre krig for

segments.body: Five Russian glide bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 20 people, including four children, and injuring at least 32, Ukrainian officials said. Rescue workers searched damaged buildings for people believed to be trapped. The city is less than 10 miles from the front line.

segments.title: Fuel, sanctions and pressure
segments.body: The attack came hours after Donald Trump announced a deal to allow Russian diesel exports, saying it would help address high fuel prices. Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the agreement a gift to Vladimir Putin and argued that easing pressure would help Russia continue the war. Trump then said Ukraine needed a new leader and urged Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian refineries.

perspectives.body: Oil analyst Arne Lohmann Rasmussen said the announced diesel volumes were small relative to global demand and unlikely to bring prices back to pre-Iran-war levels. He said the deal could still help Russia fund its war.

segments.title: Allies remain divided
segments.body: The UK prime minister expressed solidarity with Zelenskyy and called for continued pressure on Russia. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the deal would provide Moscow with more revenue and said European foreign ministers planned a new sanctions package. The fuel arrangement’s terms and potential impact on prices remain disputed.

content.headline: Myanmar junta conscription drive fuels reports of abductions and recruitment-for
content.shortHeadline: Reports of forced recruitment grow in Myanmar
content.standfirst: Young people in Myanmar describe fear of being taken for military service as the junta struggles to meet recruitment quotas. A BBC investigation reports allegations of coercion, extortion and the sale of recruits between local authorities.

image.caption: A young man in Myanmar is among those at risk of forced recruitment, according to the report.

sources.originalTitle: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army

segments.body: In Hpa-An, young people and their families say they are afraid of being seized and forced into military service. The BBC reports that junta authorities have been ordered to meet recruitment quotas as the military faces resistance from ethnic militias and pro-democracy forces.

segments.title: A system under pressure
segments.body: A former military officer who joined the anti-coup movement told the BBC that recruits were being tracked, detained and sometimes sold between local administrative areas to fill quotas. The junta did not comment on the allegations. The reporting also describes families fleeing or keeping young people indoors, while coercive recruitment adds to displacement and labour shortages.

content.headline: Nobel laureate condemns US sanctions on International Criminal Court
content.shortHeadline: Nobel laureate calls US ICC sanctions unacceptable
content.standfirst: Navi Pillay, awarded this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, said sanctions against the International Criminal Court were an attack on judges for their decisions. The US says the measures defend its sovereignty.

image.caption: Navi Pillay, former ICC judge and Nobel Peace Prize laureate.

sources.originalTitle: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
Trump raser over Nobels fredspris: En skamplet på Norges omdømme

segments.body: Navi Pillay, a former International Criminal Court judge and this year’s Nobel Peace Prize laureate, called US sanctions on the court “unheard of” and “unacceptable”. The measures target the ICC as an institution and restrict US entities from making transactions with it.

segments.title: A dispute over the court’s authority
segments.body: The Trump administration says the sanctions defend US sovereignty and objects to the court’s past investigation of US actions in Afghanistan and arrest warrants for Israeli officials. The ICC says the measures threaten the rule of law. The UK and several other countries said they regretted and strongly disagreed with the sanctions.

perspectives.body: Trump criticised Pillay’s selection and called the Nobel committee’s decision a stain on Norway. The report also notes that the US announced sanctions against the ICC hours after the prize was awarded.

content.headline: Drone strike kills 41 people at displaced people’s gathering in Sudan
content.shortHeadline: Rights group says Sudan drone strike killed 41
content.standfirst: A strike in Sudan’s Blue Nile region killed 41 people, including eight children, at a gathering of displaced people, the rights group Emergency Lawyers said. The area had reportedly faced repeated attacks.

sources.originalTitle: Drone strike by Sudan paramilitary kills 41 near Ethiopian border, rights group says

segments.body: Emergency Lawyers said a drone attack by Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces struck a gathering of displaced people in the Abu Shandi area of Blue Nile state, near Ethiopia, killing 41. The group said eight children were among those killed. The UN humanitarian coordination office said initial reports suggested most casualties were women and children.

segments.title: A deepening humanitarian crisis
segments.body: Sudan’s army and the RSF have fought for power since 2023. The conflict has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million people, according to the report. The UN said the area struck had been under sustained attack in recent weeks, displacing thousands more.

content.headline: Pentagon plan to livestream military execution draws criticism
content.shortHeadline: US plan to livestream execution faces criticism
content.standfirst: The Pentagon says the planned December firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, will be livestreamed. The proposal has drawn objections, while legal challenges could delay it.

image.caption: Nidal Malik Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on 3 December.

sources.originalTitle: Pentagon: Henrettelse af mand bag massedrab på militærbase skal livestreames
Vance vil ikke se livestream af planlagt henrettelse i USA
Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attempt

segments.body: The Pentagon says it plans to livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 at Fort Hood in 2009. The execution is scheduled for 3 December, though experts said legal challenges could delay it.

segments.title: Debate over public executions
segments.body: The announcement has renewed debate about making an execution public. Vice-President J.D. Vance said he would not watch if it is streamed, and Republican senator Thom Tillis called the idea “more than repulsive”. Researchers and critics interviewed by the BBC questioned whether the proposal reflects public attitudes to capital punishment.

perspectives.body: Historian and capital-punishment researchers told the BBC that public executions in the US ended after a 1936 hanging drew a crowd estimated at 20,000. They warned that livestreaming could turn an execution into entertainment, though public opinion on the current proposal is not yet known.

content.headline: US investigates broadcasters after White House pool coverage boycott
content.shortHeadline: US probes broadcasters over White House coverage boycott
content.standfirst: The Justice Department is investigating whether five television networks violated competition law after they suspended shared coverage when the White House barred several outlets. Critics say the probe risks intimidating news organisations.

image.caption: The Justice Department is investigating broadcasters over their shared White House coverage.

sources.originalTitle: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
US justice department investigating TV networks over Trump pool coverage
Amerikansk ministerium efterforsker tv-stationer efter boykot af Trump

segments.body: The US Justice Department has asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News for communications about the White House television press pool. The inquiry follows a temporary halt to shared coverage after the administration blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.

segments.title: Access and press freedom
segments.body: The White House restored the outlets’ access after a judge ruled in their favour. The Justice Department says it is investigating whether the broadcasters’ joint action amounted to an illegal group boycott. The Committee to Protect Journalists criticised the inquiry, saying antitrust investigations should not be used to intimidate outlets defending access.

perspectives.body: The Guardian describes the press pool as a proxy for a broader dispute over who controls journalists’ access to the president and the content of news coverage.

content.headline: Trump meeting with election denier raises concerns over midterm oversight
content.shortHeadline: Trump meeting with election denier raises midterm concerns
content.standfirst: A former Trump administration official said the president met Tina Peters to discuss election plans. The White House did not confirm the meeting, and the reported proposals to control ballots have not been substantiated.

image.caption: Donald Trump has made claims of election fraud ahead of the US midterms.

source.credit: Foto: Annabelle Gordon / Pool / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Møde i Det Hvide Hus forstærker frygt for, at Trump planlægger at blande sig i valget

segments.body: Ed Martin, a former Trump administration official, said Tina Peters met Donald Trump at the White House to discuss the coming midterm elections. Peters, a former Colorado county election official, was convicted over unlawful access to election equipment and later released early after pressure from Trump. The White House declined to confirm the reported meeting.

segments.title: Claims and preparations
segments.body: Peters’ lawyer described a plan to take control of ballots for a recount, but the report says Peters did not document fraud in 2020 and experts have found no evidence that such fraud occurred. Democrats say they are preparing for possible attempts to challenge or interfere with the midterm process. The reported discussion does not establish that any intervention is planned.

content.headline: MPs seek to overturn ruling limiting civil claims against police
content.shortHeadline: MPs challenge police immunity ruling
content.standfirst: A cross-party amendment would restrict police immunity in civil claims involving grave investigative failings, including fabricated evidence or reckless disclosure. The move follows a case in which a domestic abuse victim’s refuge address was disclosed.

sources.originalTitle: Bid to overturn ruling which stops police being sued for failings

segments.body: Andrew Mitchell and Jess Phillips have proposed an amendment to limit the effect of a 2025 Court of Appeal ruling on police immunity in England and Wales. They want exceptions where officers are alleged to have fabricated evidence, acted dishonestly or negligently, or recklessly disclosed confidential information.

segments.title: The case behind the challenge
segments.body: The ruling arose from a domestic abuse victim’s claim after Sussex Police included her secret refuge address in a file sent to prosecutors. A prosecutor later disclosed the address in court, forcing the woman to flee again. Police can still face criminal prosecution and misconduct proceedings; a separate Supreme Court appeal could also overturn the ruling.

content.headline: Camden was warned about nursery worker three years before his arrest
content.shortHeadline: Nursery worker was cleared after earlier safeguarding concerns
content.standfirst: The Guardian reports that Camden council advised a nursery to investigate concerns about Vincent Chan in 2021, and he was allowed back into a child-facing role. Chan later pleaded guilty to 56 offences and was jailed for 18 years.

image.caption: Vincent Chan was jailed for 18 years after pleading guilty to offences against children.

sources.originalTitle: Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest

segments.body: Vincent Chan was the subject of safeguarding concerns raised with his nursery in 2021, three years before his arrest. The Guardian reports that Camden council advised Bright Horizons to investigate; Chan was temporarily moved away from children and then cleared to return to his role.

segments.title: Questions about oversight
segments.body: Chan later pleaded guilty to 56 offences, including sexual assaults on young children at the nursery, and was sentenced to 18 years in prison. Camden commissioned an independent safeguarding review, now expected in early 2027. The council says the review is intended to help prevent future abuse; Bright Horizons says it cannot comment while the process continues.

content.headline: Plan 2 graduates describe debts that rise despite repayments
content.shortHeadline: Why some graduates’ Plan 2 debts keep growing
content.standfirst: Three university friends who took out similar loans have seen sharply different outcomes: one cleared her balance, while two still owe tens of thousands. Their stories come amid renewed debate over Plan 2 repayment terms.

image.caption: Lizzy, Charlotte and Libby studied at the University of Newcastle from 2012.

sources.originalTitle: Three friends on their student debt: one paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up

segments.body: Charlotte, Libby and Lizzy each borrowed about £37,500 for tuition and living costs after starting university in 2012. Charlotte earns about £50,000 but says interest has outpaced her repayments; Libby’s balance has stayed near £47,000, while on maternity leave her repayments have fallen.

segments.title: Different choices, different costs
segments.body: Lizzy, who earns £85,000, repaid her loan early with help from family and estimates that doing so will save about £20,000. Financial journalist Holly Mead cautions that voluntary overpayments are not right for everyone: smaller payments may simply mean paying interest that would otherwise be written off after 30 years.

segments.title: Policy under scrutiny
segments.body: Plan 2 loans were issued in England from 2012 and are still used in Wales. Campaigners oppose a freeze to the repayment threshold, saying it would make graduates pay sooner and more each month. The government says it is working to make the system fairer and has promised clearer information for applicants.

content.headline: Councils face a prolonged Right to Buy backlog as house sales rise
content.shortHeadline: Right to Buy backlog threatens council housebuilding plans
content.standfirst: An analysis by the i Paper finds councils are on track to sell more homes than the government expects to replace in the coming years. Local authorities say a backlog of applications is prolonging the loss of social housing.

image.caption: The analysis compares projected Right to Buy sales with expected replacement homes.

sources.originalTitle: Council housebuilding plan thrown into disarray by Right to Buy surge

segments.body: Right to Buy sales rose 90% last year after discounts were cut in 2024, and a backlog of applications means councils expect sales to remain high. The i Paper’s analysis finds more than 14,000 homes may be sold this year and next, compared with 10,450 replacements forecast by the government.

segments.title: A disputed route to replacement
segments.body: Councils say they cannot replace homes quickly enough, and some argue sale receipts do not cover the cost of building new ones. The housing ministry says reforms and £39bn in social and affordable housing investment will help councils build more homes than are sold over the next decade.

content.headline: UK review warns ADHD diagnoses may approach prevalence estimates
content.shortHeadline: Review warns ADHD diagnoses are rising sharply
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says diagnosis rates among some young people are nearing or exceeding estimated prevalence, but stresses that the findings do not prove widespread overdiagnosis. Experts disagree on the causes and risks.

image.caption: The report examines rising rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis
How claims of ‘masking’ in ADHD are impacting diagnosis

segments.body: A government review found that 5% of teenage boys had an ADHD diagnosis last year, up from 2% a decade earlier; among girls, the rate rose from 0.5% to 2.5%. The report says NHS rates for some groups are approaching or exceeding estimated prevalence, but does not establish that overdiagnosis is happening at scale.

segments.title: What the rise may mean
segments.body: The review and experts point to several possible drivers: changing definitions and awareness, subjective assessments, private clinics and increased use of diagnosis to access support. Some specialists warn that overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis may be growing; others stress that people who need assessment can still face long waits and remain undiagnosed.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s separate report focuses on “masking”: some clinicians say coping strategies can hide ADHD symptoms, while critics call the concept difficult to test. Researchers say evidence on masking in ADHD remains at an early stage.

content.headline: Pharmacy closures leave some patients facing long trips for medicines
content.shortHeadline: Pharmacy closures widen access gaps in England
content.standfirst: Fifty-one high-street pharmacies in England closed between January and August, including 31 supported to serve areas with limited access. Some patients now face lengthy journeys for prescriptions and advice.

image.caption: More than 50 pharmacies in England closed in the first eight months of the year.

sources.originalTitle: The worst places to live if you are ill – where trips to chemists take an hour

segments.body: Analysis by the National Pharmacy Association found that 51 pharmacies in England closed between January and August, including 31 branches receiving support intended to protect access in areas with few alternatives. The report estimates that 9.9 million people have seen a local pharmacy close since 2016.

segments.title: The impact on patients
segments.body: In Long Rock, near Penzance, a closure left some patients facing a 17-mile round trip and up to 80 minutes by public transport to reach another pharmacy. Pharmacy representatives say funding has not kept pace with costs; the government announced a £340m funding increase in May, but the sector says a substantial gap remains.

content.headline: Thousands march in London for Palestinians; police report 20 arrests
content.shortHeadline: Thousands attend pro-Palestinian march in London
content.standfirst: Protesters called for the UK to stop supplying arms to Israel as the Metropolitan Police reported 20 arrests. Organisers gave a much higher attendance estimate than the police or independent counts in the report.

image.caption: Pro-Palestinian demonstrators gather in London.

sources.originalTitle: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’

segments.body: Thousands gathered in central London and marched towards Parliament in support of Palestinians. The Metropolitan Police said 20 people were arrested, including in connection with criminal damage, alleged support for a proscribed organisation and assaults on officers. Organisers said 250,000 people attended.

segments.title: A changed political backdrop
segments.body: The march was the first national demonstration since the UK government announced sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and said it considers Israel’s occupation of the West Bank unlawful. Protesters called for an end to UK arms supplies to Israel; the report also describes continuing attacks in Gaza and the West Bank.

content.headline: BBC cuts raise fears of losing experienced news and programme staff
content.shortHeadline: BBC staff fear cuts will deepen talent drain
content.standfirst: More than 2,000 jobs are expected to go as the BBC seeks to save £500m. Staff quoted by the i Paper warn that voluntary redundancies could take experienced workers to competitors as morale falls.

image.caption: More than 2,000 BBC jobs are expected to go as the corporation seeks savings.

sources.originalTitle: BBC faces losing its best talent from news and sport as a result of savage cuts

segments.body: The BBC plans more than 2,000 job cuts across television and radio as it seeks £500m in savings amid falling licence-fee income. Staff quoted by the i Paper say voluntary redundancy risks prompting skilled colleagues to leave for commercial rivals.

segments.title: Programming and leadership changes
segments.body: The BBC has announced cuts to several Radio 4 programmes, including You and Yours, Thinking Allowed and Free Thinking. BBC leaders say the decisions are difficult and are intended to save money while investing for the future; some staff and former presenters argue the cuts could weaken public-service reporting.

perspectives.body: One example in the report is Balkans correspondent Guy De Launey, whose contract was not renewed, but who was later asked to cover a major regional story. The case illustrates staff concerns about how the cuts are being managed.

content.headline: Danish data breach exposes CPR access weaknesses at 1,039 companies
content.shortHeadline: CPR breach prompts security warning to 1,039 companies
content.standfirst: A hacker accessed nearly 8.8 million Danish personal identification numbers through a company with CPR register access. The government has sent new security requirements to more than 1,000 firms.

image.caption: A graphic illustrating a password linked to the CPR register breach.

sources.originalTitle: Afsløring: Fynsk virksomhed er centrum for massivt CPR-databrud
1039 virksomheder har fået indskærpet sikkerhed efter CPR-læk

segments.body: A breach involving a software company in Funen exposed access to nearly 8.8 million CPR numbers, according to reporting by DR and Politiken. The CPR administration said the access was used over a period of 21 days and 17 hours before it was blocked. No suspect has been charged.

segments.title: Security requirements tightened
segments.body: The government has sent letters to 1,039 companies with access to the CPR register, reminding them to appoint a security officer, monitor staff access and check monthly transaction volumes. The government has acknowledged that security around the system was not good enough and requested a security review.

perspectives.body: DR’s investigation reports that a password exposed in an earlier data leak may have helped the attacker gain access. The outlet says it could not confirm that this specific login was used in the breach.

content.headline: Denmark plans domestic-violence strategy, but groups say funding is inadequate
content.shortHeadline: Domestic-violence strategy faces funding criticism
content.standfirst: The government has proposed DKK175m over four years for a national strategy on partner violence and killings. Support organisations say the increase over current funding may not meet demand for helplines and counselling.

image.caption: Maria Kronholm fled an abusive relationship in 2019 and later wrote about her experience.

sources.originalTitle: Regeringens plan mod partnervold kritiseres for at mangle penge
Offer for partnervold om økonomien i regeringens plan: 'Meget lidt, når man tænker på, hvad prisen kan være'

segments.body: The government plans to spend DKK175m from 2027 to 2030 on a national strategy to address partner violence and partner killings, which account for one in five killings in Denmark, according to DR. That would be about DKK9.75m more per year than the previous four-year plan.

segments.title: Demand for help
segments.body: Danner says there is a ten-month wait for one counselling service. Lev Uden Vold says nearly 4,500 people who called its national hotline last year could not get through. The organisations welcome a national strategy but say existing services need more resources.

segments.title: A survivor’s account
segments.body: Maria Kronholm, who survived years of abuse and eventually fled with help from a nurse and her father, says people in frontline roles need better training and victims need timely crisis support. She called the proposed funding too little given the potential cost of partner killings.

content.headline: Venstre politician challenges EU-backed cull of sika deer
content.shortHeadline: Sika deer cull sparks dispute over EU rules
content.standfirst: A Venstre MP says there is no evidence that sika deer in Jægersborg Dyrehave have crossbred with native deer. Denmark’s environment minister says the country must follow EU rules and does not qualify for an exemption.

sources.originalTitle: Politiker vil have minister til at stoppe udryddelse af sikahjorte

segments.body: Sika deer have lived in Jægersborg Dyrehave for about a century, but are now designated an invasive species under EU rules and are being culled. Venstre MP Marie Brixtofte argues there is no documented evidence of crossbreeding with native deer in the park.

segments.title: No exemption planned
segments.body: Environment minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen says he understands that the EU’s rationale may not fit Danish conditions, and that Denmark voted against the listing. But he says the country does not meet the conditions for an exemption and is obliged to comply with the rules. The cull continues.

content.headline: Police report details delays before rescue of kidnapped 13-year-old
content.shortHeadline: Report details delays before girl was found alive
content.standfirst: An internal review describes how technical delays in obtaining surveillance footage and a mistaken burial theory affected the search for a missing 13-year-old. A later review by experienced investigators has been ordered.

sources.originalTitle: Intern redegørelse giver nye detaljer om politi i vildrede inden anholdelse af Philip Westh

segments.body: A police review says more than ten hours passed between officers viewing surveillance footage near Kirkerup and investigators seeing it at the station. Technical problems delayed access to files that showed the convicted kidnapper’s car passing shortly before three other vehicles.

segments.title: A changing line of inquiry
segments.body: Investigators initially focused on a couple arrested nearby and searched their garden, where they believed the girl might have been buried. That theory was abandoned after the search found no burial, and police then moved to arrest Philip Westh. Officers found the girl alive at his home.

segments.title: Changes after the case
segments.body: The police district acknowledged that the time taken to secure video and make the arrest appeared long, particularly given the victim’s situation. It says it has introduced new documentation and equipment for collecting surveillance footage. The justice minister has ordered experienced investigators from other districts and the national serious-crime unit to review the investigation.

content.headline: Handheld phone use accounted for nearly one in four Danish driving points
content.shortHeadline: Handheld phones behind nearly a quarter of driving points
content.standfirst: Danish drivers received 20,910 penalty points for using handheld phones while driving in 2025, the highest number in four years. The figures may also reflect changes in police enforcement and equipment.

image.caption: An archive image accompanying the report on handheld phone use while driving.

source.credit: Foto: Ida GuldbÃ¦k Arentsen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: 20.910 klip i kørekortet for håndholdt mobil

segments.body: Police data show that 20,910 penalty points were issued for handheld phone use while driving in Denmark in 2025—about one in four of all points issued for traffic offences. The total was 7.5% higher than in 2024 and averaged 57 points a day.

segments.title: A caution on the figures
segments.body: Road-safety representatives warn that phones divert drivers’ attention, but say the increase in penalties could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment. Using a handheld phone while driving brings a penalty point and a fine; the restriction also applies when a vehicle is stopped in traffic or at a red light.

content.headline: Solanke's late leveller deepens pressure on Carrick as 10-man Spurs draw
content.shortHeadline: Late Spurs leveller deepens pressure on Carrick
content.standfirst: Dominic Solanke's added-time goal earned Tottenham a 1-1 draw at Old Trafford after Rodrigo Bentancur was sent off. Manchester United have now failed to beat 10-man opponents in successive home league games.

image.caption: Dominic Solanke scores in added time as 10-man Tottenham draw with Manchester United.

sources.originalTitle: Boos, anguish & fading belief -'worrying day' for under-pressure Carrick
'I kissed Rodrigo and said thanks' - De Zerbi 'liked' Spurs red card

segments.body: Bryan Mbeumo put United ahead, but Tottenham equalised through Solanke in added time despite playing with 10 men after Bentancur was sent off for headbutting Luke Shaw. United have six points from their first six league games and are winless in four.

segments.title: A response for Spurs, more questions for United
segments.body: United manager Michael Carrick said his side needed to be more stubborn and stronger in seeing out games, while insisting he still believes in his players. The result continues a difficult start: United have failed to win five of their six league matches.

Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi called Bentancur's reaction a mistake but said he welcomed the character it showed. He said Spurs played with more courage and energy after going down to 10, and saw the performance as a starting point for building a team.

perspectives.body: De Zerbi said he thanked Bentancur after the match, explaining that Tottenham needed a show of character and should not simply accept defeat. He also said Spurs had not yet become a team, despite the spirit they showed at Old Trafford.

content.headline: Henderson brace and Caicedo control help Chelsea beat Bournemouth 5-1
content.shortHeadline: Henderson and Caicedo drive Chelsea's 5-1 win
content.standfirst: Jordan Henderson scored twice and set up another as Chelsea recorded their most complete performance of the season. His first midfield start alongside Moises Caicedo also offered manager Xabi Alonso a possible source of balance.

image.caption: Jordan Henderson stars as Chelsea put five past Bournemouth.

sources.originalTitle: The rock behind Chelsea's entertainers: Midfield duo key for Blues

segments.body: Henderson scored after 66 seconds, assisted Morgan Rogers' goal and later added a 25-yard free-kick as Chelsea beat Bournemouth 5-1. It was his first time scoring for the club, and he became the third-oldest Chelsea player to score and assist in the same match.

segments.title: A possible midfield solution
segments.body: In their first match together, Caicedo and Henderson gave Chelsea greater control, with Caicedo making and winning more tackles than any Chelsea player and recording the team's best pass-completion rate. Chelsea still conceded from poor set-piece defending and have yet to keep a league clean sheet.

content.headline: Guimaraes wins it for Arsenal as Hincapie injury adds to concerns
content.shortHeadline: Guimaraes wins it; Arsenal await news on Hincapie
content.standfirst: Arsenal came from behind to beat Leeds 2-1 and move level on points with Manchester City, but defender Piero Hincapie was carried off after the match. The severity of his injury was not yet clear.

image.caption: Arsenal come from behind to beat Leeds at the Emirates Stadium.

sources.originalTitle: Hincapie injury adds to Arsenal issues after Guimaraes rescue act
Who changed the game? - player ratings for Arsenal v Leeds

segments.body: Leeds led through James Justin before Riccardo Calafiori equalised and Bruno Guimaraes, on as a substitute, scored the winner. It was Arsenal's fifth win in six league games and Guimaraes' second decisive contribution from the bench in three matches.

segments.title: An anxious wait after the win
segments.body: Hincapie was carried off during the post-match warm-down, clutching his right ankle. The extent of the injury remains unknown. Arsenal have conceded five goals in six league games and have fallen behind in three of their past four, despite taking important points from difficult matches.

content.headline: Renshaw's 190 puts Australia in control against South Africa
content.shortHeadline: Renshaw's 190 puts Australia on top in Durban
content.standfirst: Matt Renshaw made his first Test century in more than nine years, scoring a career-best 190 as Australia recovered from 124-6 to make 390. South Africa were 27-1 when bad light stopped play on day two.

image.caption: Matt Renshaw celebrates his first Test century in more than nine years.

sources.originalTitle: Middlesbrough-born Renshaw's epic 190 lifts Australia

segments.body: Renshaw's 397-ball innings helped Australia reach 390 all out in Durban, after they had slumped to 124-6. He built an 86-run stand with captain Pat Cummins and a 134-run partnership with Nathan Lyon, helping put Australia in control of the first Test.

segments.title: A statement innings, with selection still to come
segments.body: The 30-year-old's century strengthens his case for a regular place after an in-and-out international career. How Australia fit him into the order remains unresolved: Cameron Green is expected back, and Renshaw was moved to number five for this Test after Green was ruled out.

content.headline: Ronaldo provisionally suspended by Portuguese FA after leaving camp
content.shortHeadline: Ronaldo provisionally suspended by Portugal FA
content.standfirst: Cristiano Ronaldo faces a disciplinary process after leaving Portugal's international camp in September. The Portuguese Football Federation says the case is urgent, but the outcome and any final sanction remain undecided.

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo, a five-time Ballon d'Or winner.

sources.originalTitle: Ronaldo provisionally suspended by Portuguese FA

segments.body: The Portuguese Football Federation said it issued a provisional suspension on 9 October after Ronaldo left the squad. Its rules allow a ban of one to six months, as well as a fine, for a player who fails to report or walks out on international duty.

segments.title: A dispute over his role
segments.body: Ronaldo said he left after learning he would not start against Denmark, having been an unused substitute against Norway. He accused coach Jorge Jesus of breaking his word, later apologised to team-mates and supporters, and said he deserved punishment. The FPF says a normal disciplinary process will follow and expressed a desire to have its captain back.

content.headline: All Blacks retain Bledisloe Cup with dominant win over Australia
content.shortHeadline: All Blacks retain Bledisloe Cup for 23rd straight year
content.standfirst: New Zealand pulled away after half-time at Eden Park to retain the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd consecutive year. The win ended a three-match losing run; Australia suffered their first defeat under coach Les Kiss.

image.caption: New Zealand have not lost at Eden Park in 32 years.

sources.originalTitle: All Blacks power past Australia to retain Bledisloe Cup

segments.body: Australia were 17-14 behind at half-time, but New Zealand scored five tries after the break to pull clear. Seven All Blacks crossed in total, with Damian McKenzie adding 15 points from kicks.

segments.title: A remarkable run at Eden Park
segments.body: The All Blacks have not lost at the Auckland venue since 1994 and have now gone 54 Tests unbeaten there. Australia had been seeking their first Eden Park win since 1986; the teams meet again in Sydney on 17 October.

content.headline: Late Ipswich comeback leaves Fulham bottom and winless in six
content.shortHeadline: Late Ipswich goals deepen Fulham's difficult start
content.standfirst: Fulham led at Ipswich but conceded twice after the 88th minute to lose 2-1. They remain winless after six league games, with manager Alvaro Arbeloa insisting he is not afraid of the pressure.

image.caption: Ipswich come from behind to beat Fulham.

sources.originalTitle: Arbeloa 'doesn't feel fear' but pressure increases after loss

segments.body: Ryan Sessegnon put Fulham ahead, but Ipswich scored twice in the closing minutes to claim a 2-1 win. It was the second successive league match in which Fulham had led late and then conceded; they have two points and sit bottom.

segments.title: Arbeloa says the focus is on points
segments.body: Arbeloa said he did not worry about his position and did not feel fear, but accepted that Fulham needed points. His side have conceded in the final 15 minutes in four of their six league matches. Ryan Sessegnon said the team needed to demand more of itself.

content.headline: Naderi double sends Rangers top after sixth straight league win
content.shortHeadline: Naderi double sends Rangers top of the Premiership
content.standfirst: Ryan Naderi scored twice as Rangers beat Kilmarnock to extend their league winning run to six and move a point clear at the top. The striker has found form after a slow start to his Rangers career.

image.caption: Rangers striker Ryan Naderi has helped the club win seven matches in a row in all competitions.

sources.originalTitle: 'Reminds me of Muller' - Naderi proving worth in Rangers revival

segments.body: Naderi's first-half double helped Rangers beat Kilmarnock and rise to the top of the Scottish Premiership. It was their sixth straight league win and seventh in all competitions; Celtic could reclaim top spot when they play on Sunday.

segments.title: A striker finding his stride
segments.body: Naderi now has three goals in his past two league games, after scoring the winner against Celtic before the international break. He has stepped up while Lawrence Shankland and Youssef Chermiti are injured, though manager Derek McInnes said Rangers' second-half display against Kilmarnock was below the required standard.

content.headline: Punk at 50: musicians around the world explain what the genre means to them
content.shortHeadline: Punk at 50: a global outlet for anger, freedom and community
content.standfirst: From Ukraine and Morocco to South Africa and Greenland, musicians describe punk as a way to challenge authority, claim space and find one another. Their accounts show how a genre born in rebellion keeps changing with its surroundings.

image.caption: Musicians from Beton, Twenty One Children, Taqbir and Depustūtes.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their lives

segments.body: For musicians interviewed as punk turns 50, it is less a fixed sound than a way to question the world and make room for yourself in it. In Ukraine, Beton vocalist Andriy Zholob recalls playing guitar on the frontline while serving as a surgeon; the band later recorded “Kyiv Calling” to raise money for Ukrainian resistance.

segments.title: A scene shaped by place
segments.body: Moroccan-born Taqbir vocalist Nao describes performing anonymously before moving to Spain, where punk helped her reconcile being Muslim, gay and herself. In Soweto, Twenty One Children connect their music to police harassment, community work and a DIY skate park; in Wuhan, SMZB’s Wu Wei recalls authorities prohibiting performances and taking albums offline.

segments.title: A shared language, not a single story
segments.body: The musicians’ experiences differ, but many describe punk as permission to question norms and turn frustration into something collective. In Riga, Depustūtes singer Evisa Petrovska says singing in Latvian lets her address local politics and expectations placed on women; Greenland’s Uummat see the scene as small, but have built an audience of their own.

content.headline: Stevie Wonder’s four-song EP opens a rare window on his 1970s vault
content.shortHeadline: Stevie Wonder’s new EP offers four vault recordings
content.standfirst: Released on the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life, the four outtakes were selected by Wonder and mixed by the original album’s engineers. The review finds them illuminating without diminishing the landmark record.

sources.originalTitle: Songs in the Key of Life - The EP

segments.body: Songs in the Key of Life EP gathers four recordings from sessions around Stevie Wonder’s 1976 album. Three songs had been known only by title, according to the review; the fourth, “I Can See the Sun in Late December”, had been recorded by Roberta Flack and performed by Wonder before. Here, a fuller, quicker arrangement shifts it toward a celebration of everyday life.

segments.title: An addendum, not a revision
segments.body: The other tracks return to familiar parts of Wonder’s musical language: buoyant early-70s-style romance, devotional funk and an easy, Latin-inflected groove. The reviewer argues that issuing the songs separately preserves the original album’s sense of completion while offering a glimpse of the work left in the vault.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall album turns a fraught performance into song
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance, preserved live
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo set pairs three unreleased songs with reworked material from Heavy Metal. The review hears a more fluid performer emerging in a recording that captures the concert while also building its own mythology.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Recorded at Carnegie Hall in December 2025, Cameron Winter’s solo album presents a piano-led performance that sounds more open than the difficult studio process behind his 2024 debut, Heavy Metal. The review singles out “Try As I May”, transformed from a more plodding recorded version into a song that seems to breathe with Winter’s playing.

segments.title: New songs, new scale
segments.body: Three unreleased songs are among the night’s highlights. The review describes “If You Turn Back Now” as an especially powerful culmination, while the concert film—premiered at the New York Film Festival—shows Winter’s nerves and intense concentration. Together, the album and film preserve the evening while shaping it into a story about an artist learning to inhabit the stage.

content.headline: Dawn Richard’s Creole Culture makes New Orleans music a living inheritance
content.shortHeadline: Dawn Richard’s New Orleans-rooted Creole Culture
content.standfirst: The third album in Richard’s New Orleans trilogy blends programmed beats, live playing and local musical references. The review welcomes its communal energy but finds the songwriting less adventurous than her best work.

sources.originalTitle: creole culture

segments.body: On Creole Culture, Dawn Richard turns from the more experimental pop and R&B of earlier work toward a more understated celebration of New Orleans. The review hears a record built around intimate musical connections rather than novelty, following the earlier albums New Breed and Second Line: An Electro Revival.

segments.title: A parade in motion
segments.body: Live instrumentation and co-production with Los Angeles jazz ensemble Katalyst Collective give the songs momentum. A track can travel from conversational Creole audio through drums and amapiano into gospel; elsewhere, a Chocolate Milk song co-written by Richard’s father is reworked with jungle breaks. The album’s transitions make it feel, the review suggests, like a DJ set.

segments.title: Roots and risk
segments.body: The review finds the record’s homespun pride appealing, but says its grounded approach sometimes lacks the eccentric imagination and risk that distinguished Richard’s earlier albums. Its central strength, in this reading, is the way it holds cultural inheritance as both rooted and continually in motion.

content.headline: Helen’s Linda’s Head finds Liz Harris singing more plainly—and with joy
content.shortHeadline: Helen’s Linda’s Head brings Liz Harris into sharper focus
content.standfirst: On the second album from the trio led by Grouper’s Liz Harris, vocals and lyrics come forward without losing the band’s enveloping shoegaze sound. The review hears melancholy, playfulness and the pleasure of making music together.

sources.originalTitle: Linda’s Head

segments.body: Helen’s second album, Linda’s Head, arrives more than a decade after The Original Faces. Where the debut often submerged Liz Harris’s voice in the trio’s sound, this record brings her lyrics into clearer view while keeping the spaciousness and haze associated with her work as Grouper.

segments.title: A wider emotional range
segments.body: The songs look skyward, moving among stars, storms and distant horizons. The review hears both yearning and delight: Harris’s voice can hover over a forceful bass line, while the three musicians’ interplay gives even the darker material a sense of shared momentum. The album closes with thunder samples that bring its natural imagery into focus.

content.headline: Victoria Monét’s Frequency of Love aims for a bigger, softer kind of R&B
content.shortHeadline: Victoria Monét’s expansive, romantic Frequency of Love
content.standfirst: Monét follows her Grammy-winning breakthrough with a 22-track exploration of devotion, ballads and retro R&B. The review admires her range and polish, while questioning whether the sprawling album’s many ideas cohere.

sources.originalTitle: Frequency of Love

segments.body: Frequency of Love moves Victoria Monét away from the confident party persona of the Jaguar albums and toward a more openly romantic voice. The review highlights the change in tone: earnest declarations of commitment sit alongside flashes of the wit and sexual confidence that have long been part of her writing.

segments.title: A grand, sometimes crowded design
segments.body: The production ranges from quiet-storm ballads to cinematic strings and contemporary R&B, with a Kaytranada collaboration among its stylistic turns. The review praises Monét’s versatility and meticulous performances, but argues that 22 tracks and a frequently similar muted backdrop can make some songs blur together. The scale is compelling, if not always focused.

content.headline: Lambchop’s Punching the Clown pares back the sound but keeps its stories unruly
content.shortHeadline: Lambchop’s Punching the Clown finds new intimacy
content.standfirst: Kurt Wagner’s long-running band pares its arrangements back to acoustic guitar, banjo and choir, making room for stories that veer between tenderness, absurdity and unease. The review finds the stripped-down approach emotionally direct rather than merely nostalgic.

sources.originalTitle: Punching the Clown

segments.body: Lambchop have repeatedly changed musical direction, but Kurt Wagner’s writing remains difficult to pin down. On Punching the Clown, sparse acoustic arrangements, banjo and choir frame his shifting stories without tidying away their digressions, jokes or unsettling details.

segments.title: The strange details matter
segments.body: The review finds the simplest setting a particularly effective one for Wagner’s songs. “The New World Wave” stretches across generations, while “To Do” turns an ordinary task into a reminder of unfinished life. Elsewhere, comic turns and abrupt changes in tone sit beside illness, death and political anxiety, making the record feel both disquieting and unusually direct.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue reveals an album that never stood still
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s many versions come into view in a lavish reissue
content.standfirst: A new expanded edition gathers stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and material from both the UK and US releases. The review treats the extras not as proof of one definitive album, but as a reminder of how music, technology and commerce shaped it.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The new Rubber Soul edition places the Beatles’ 1965 album alongside outtakes, recording notes and both UK and US versions. The review revisits the record as a turning point in pop, while stressing how quickly it was made: tracking wrapped in November and the album reached shops in December.

segments.title: One album, many perspectives
segments.body: The US release replaced some livelier songs with more subdued tracks, and the set includes different stereo and mono mixes. The review finds meaning in those variations, as well as in the unfinished takes and studio fragments: they show a band making choices under pressure, not an inevitable masterpiece arriving fully formed.

segments.title: What a reissue can—and cannot—resolve
segments.body: The expanded package invites listeners to search for the moment when the album’s competing elements clicked, but the reviewer’s conclusion is that no single version is the real Rubber Soul. The reissue offers a richer account of the record’s history without replacing the different versions listeners have made their own.

content.headline: Artificial turns OpenAI’s founding into a timely film about who controls AI
content.shortHeadline: Artificial asks who gets to control AI—and its future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s drama follows the split between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever as OpenAI changes from nonprofit ideal to commercial force. The film’s release has also drawn attention to the studio’s business ties with the company.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial follows the creation and transformation of OpenAI through the fictionalised experiences of co-founders Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. Its central conflict is between idealism and commerce, and between arguments for caution over AI and the push to build and deploy it.

segments.title: A release shadowed by real-world debate
segments.body: The film includes a scene in which an AI system gets past a human-verification test. The BBC account connects that moment to reported AI-agent security incidents, while noting that the film was completed before those disclosures. Its release was also complicated when Amazon MGM declined to distribute it after Amazon announced an investment in OpenAI; Neon later acquired the film.

segments.title: A human story, with a contested portrait
segments.body: The account describes Sutskever as the film’s main character and ethical counterweight, but criticises its portrayal of Altman as underwritten. It also notes that the real Altman, who had seen the trailer but not the film, questioned its accuracy. The industry-wide question of how to manage AI, the report concludes, remains unresolved.

content.headline: Free Leonard Peltier revisits a decades-long fight over justice and Native land
content.shortHeadline: Free Leonard Peltier traces a long fight for justice
content.standfirst: The Netflix documentary follows Peltier’s imprisonment, the activism around his case and the commutation that allowed him to serve the rest of his sentence at home. Its filmmakers say they set out to examine the history and land conflict, not to resolve who fired the shots.

image.caption: Leonard Peltier outside prison after his release in February 2025.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US

segments.body: Leonard Peltier spent nearly 50 years in prison after being convicted in connection with the 1975 deaths of two FBI agents at Pine Ridge. He has always denied the killings. President Joe Biden commuted his sentence in January 2025, allowing him to serve the remainder under house arrest, but did not pardon him.

segments.title: The history around the case
segments.body: Directors David France and Jesse Short Bull build the documentary from archival material and interviews, tracing Peltier’s involvement in the American Indian Movement and the conflicts surrounding Pine Ridge. France says their aim was not to solve who pulled the trigger, but to examine the history and land disputes that, in his account, had been missing from earlier tellings.

segments.title: Commutation is not freedom
segments.body: The film also follows the disputed evidence and legal decisions that kept Peltier imprisoned, which the filmmakers and supporters describe as a miscarriage of justice. Peltier says house arrest is not full freedom and remains concerned about threats to Native communities and treaty rights.

content.headline: In the Shadows turns boxer Ramla Ali’s life into a familiar, forceful drama
content.shortHeadline: In the Shadows tells Ramla Ali’s story in the boxing ring
content.standfirst: Jasmine Jobson plays Ali as she pursues boxing in secret from a family that disapproves. The review finds a capable but conventional sports drama, strengthened by the story of the pressures Ali faced beyond the ring.

image.caption: Jasmine Jobson as boxer Ramla Ali in In the Shadows.

sources.originalTitle: In the Shadows review – true tale of Ramla Ali’s remarkable rise through the boxing ranks is a knockout

segments.body: In the Shadows follows British-Somali boxer Ramla Ali, who came to the UK as a refugee and became the first person to box for Somalia at the Olympic Games. Jasmine Jobson plays Ali in a film that moves through familiar boxing-drama scenes, from the first gym visit to her first competitive bout.

segments.title: The fight beyond the ring
segments.body: Ali has to conceal her training from her family, who would not accept boxing as a pastime for a Muslim girl. The review sees that secrecy as a meaningful difference from many other women’s boxing films, and says the film’s strongest material lies in the painful past that helps explain Ali’s determination.

content.headline: Tenzing puts Sherpa climber’s achievement at the centre of Everest’s first-summ\
content.shortHeadline: Tenzing centres the Sherpa climber in Everest’s first ascent
content.standfirst: Jennifer Peedom’s film revisits the 1953 Everest expedition with Tenzing Norgay at its centre. The review welcomes the shift in focus, while finding the drama’s treatment of the relationship with Edmund Hillary gentler than a full challenge to the imperial story.

image.caption: Tom Hiddleston and Genden Phuntsok in Tenzing.

sources.originalTitle: Tenzing review – reconstruction of first summit of Everest puts Sherpa at the centre of the story

segments.body: Tenzing retells the 1953 Everest ascent through the life of Tenzing Norgay, played by Genden Phuntsok, alongside Tom Hiddleston as Edmund Hillary. The film makes Norgay’s climbing skill and knowledge central to the expedition, rather than treating him as an assistant to the better-known New Zealander.

segments.title: A change of emphasis
segments.body: The review notes that the achievement was claimed at the time as a triumph for Hillary and the British empire. The film instead follows Norgay’s early life and his relationship with the mountain, though the critic says it stops short of a direct rebuke to imperial arrogance. Phuntsok’s performance, the review concludes, carries the film.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning’s Facebook exposé draws sharply different verdicts
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning: a Facebook exposé with divided critics
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel follows whistleblower Frances Haugen and journalist Jeff Horwitz as they expose Facebook’s internal research and practices. One review finds an entertaining but politically evasive drama; another says it lacks the urgency to change viewers’ minds.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning dramatises Frances Haugen’s disclosures about Facebook and the reporting by Jeff Horwitz that followed. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg, with Mikey Madison as Haugen and Jeremy Allen White as Horwitz. The story centres on the company’s recommendation systems, political content and the impact of its products on users.

segments.title: The disagreement is over what the film leaves out
segments.body: The Guardian review finds Sorkin’s fast-moving drama entertaining, but faults it for not naming Trump or fully reckoning with the political future beyond its 2021 setting. The i Paper review likewise sees Facebook’s influence as frightening, but argues the film’s restrained, low-conflict treatment is too mild to move an audience already aware of the company’s power.

perspectives.body: The i Paper critic focuses on the viewer’s own dependence on Meta products, arguing that the film’s account of manipulation and outrage is unsettling partly because audiences may recognise their continued use of the platforms.

content.headline: James Dean’s East of Eden performance shows the vulnerable boy behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebellious-cool image
content.standfirst: A close reading of East of Eden revisits the unscripted anger and vulnerability that made Dean a star. It argues that his enduring appeal lies less in the image of youthful rebellion than in the desperate son caught inside it.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: On the set of East of Eden, director Elia Kazan prompted James Dean to provoke co-star Raymond Massey during a scene. Massey’s anger was real, and the film kept the moment. The account uses that episode to trace Dean’s instinctive, unsettled approach to acting and the strained father-son relationship at the centre of the film.

segments.title: A short career, a lasting image
segments.body: Dean died at 24, after three starring roles, and the article considers how his posthumous reputation grew around the idea of the rebellious young star. It argues that East of Eden offers a more revealing image: a vulnerable son reaching for affection from a father who cannot return it.

content.headline: Digger’s Tom Cruise takes a risk in an eccentric climate-change satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger turns Tom Cruise into an oil baron in an eco-satire
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film casts Cruise as a wealthy oilman facing the consequences of an environmental catastrophe. The review finds its satire blunt and its performance deliberately excessive, even as it warns that the film’s scale and strangeness will divide viewers.

image.caption: Tom Cruise in prosthetic make-up as oil baron Digger Rockwell.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: In Digger, Tom Cruise plays an ageing oil billionaire whose company has helped trigger a climate-related catastrophe. The review describes a deliberately outsize performance, complete with prosthetics, as the film turns a crisis meeting into a satire of corporate evasion, political power and the effort to control the story.

segments.title: A deliberately divisive gamble
segments.body: The film’s scenario—a drifting iceberg threatening major cities—may once have seemed far-fetched, but the review finds its environmental argument newly resonant. It also says the film’s excesses and two high-concept twists make it a love-it-or-hate-it proposition, rather than a conventional star vehicle.

content.headline: Time’s third series turns its prison drama on boys locked away too young
content.shortHeadline: Time returns with a harrowing story of boys in prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s drama moves into a young offenders institution, with David Tennant as a prison officer and Siobhan Finneran returning as chaplain Marie-Louise. A review and behind-the-scenes reporting examine the series’ urgency and the conditions it depicts.

image.caption: David Tennant, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and Siobhan Finneran in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV drama
‘Me and the lads would not survive a day in here’: inside TV’s utterly stunning, Bafta-winning prison drama

segments.body: The third series of Time follows boys in a young offenders institution, with Tennant’s veteran officer Bobby Bailey and Finneran’s chaplain Marie-Louise at its centre. The Guardian review calls the opening episodes exceptionally tense and difficult to watch, as the drama places its young characters inside a system marked by violence and isolation.

segments.title: The conditions behind the drama
segments.body: In a separate set visit, McGovern and Tennant describe prisons with fewer staff and fewer opportunities for education, training and rehabilitation. McGovern says 23-hour lockdowns and restrictions on young people mixing have become more common since Covid; the reporting presents these as their concerns about the system, not as a substitute for the series’ fictional story.

perspectives.body: The set report adds testimony from McGovern and cast about the reality of prison routines, the young actors’ first visits to institutions and the importance of seeing incarcerated teenagers as children with lives beyond their sentences.

segments.title: Drama as a demand to look
segments.body: Both pieces see the series as an argument against treating young prisoners as invisible. The review urges viewers, including politicians, to confront the question of whether institutions can help children change; McGovern’s account of meeting a devastated teenager in custody underlines the human stakes of that question.

content.headline: Romola Garai on Adultery, intimacy on set and the work of playing Beth
content.shortHeadline: Romola Garai on playing a married woman in Adultery
content.standfirst: Garai discusses her role in ITV’s drama about two married people having an affair, including its portrayal of marital disappointment, desire and family life. She also explains how intimacy coordination has changed the way sex scenes are made.

image.caption: Romola Garai in Adultery.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in cars

segments.body: In Adultery, Romola Garai plays Beth, a personal trainer whose affair with GP Tom, played by Dominic Cooper, threatens two families. Garai says she hesitated over a story about an unfaithful woman written by a man, but found the scripts attentive to the ordinary disappointments and sacrifices that shape Beth’s marriage.

segments.title: On set and on screen
segments.body: Garai says sex scenes are now more carefully discussed and choreographed with intimacy coordinators, a change she contrasts with earlier work in which performers were often left without clear direction. She also hopes the drama will prompt conversations about how its characters’ choices affect spouses and children.

content.headline: Carrie’s new adaptation sparks a debate over rage, agency and fidelity
content.shortHeadline: Carrie: a new adaptation divides fans and critics
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s Prime Video series has prompted criticism over its changes to Stephen King’s heroine. One review argues the reinvention removes Carrie’s anger and agency; a BBC account sets out fans’ concerns alongside the case for modernising the story.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in the Prime Video series.

sources.originalTitle: The Carrie remake made me furious
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: The new eight-part Carrie moves King’s story into a present-day school environment. The i Paper critic, who first read the novel as a bullied teenager, argues that the adaptation makes Carrie fearful and passive where the book gives her anger and a decisive role in her revenge.

segments.title: What an adaptation owes its source
segments.body: The BBC report records fans’ objections to the casting and to a heroine who differs from King’s description, while also noting that the series updates the story for social media and contemporary school bullying. Film scholar Sorcha Ní Fhlainn argues that the new version can work on its own terms; the i Paper review sees its changes as a loss of the novel’s central force.

perspectives.body: The BBC account offers a more open verdict: it recognises the departures that have upset fans but cites academic support for the series’ modern setting and its own interpretation of Carrie’s otherness.

content.headline: Gromit will speak for the first time in Martin Freeman’s audiobook
content.shortHeadline: Martin Freeman gives Gromit an audiobook voice
content.standfirst: The famously silent Wallace & Gromit dog will narrate his autobiography in an audiobook, with Nick Park saying Freeman will read Gromit’s thoughts rather than invent a new speaking voice.

image.caption: Gromit, the silent dog from the Wallace & Gromit films.

sources.originalTitle: Gromit finally gets a voice … and it’s Martin Freeman

segments.body: After 37 years without a spoken line on screen, Gromit will be heard in an audiobook version of his autobiography, voiced by Martin Freeman. Creator Nick Park says Freeman will read the character’s inner thoughts and witticisms, rather than perform a conventional Gromit voice.

The book is one of two forthcoming franchise projects: an immersive Wallace & Gromit experience is also due to open at Lightroom in London. Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit is scheduled for publication on 22 October.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week adds a welcome edge to the tent
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off lets viewers set the challenges—and shakes things up
content.standfirst: The first audience-choice week handed challenge-setting power to viewers, producing unusual bakes and a sharper dynamic between judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. The review sees a small but promising break from the show’s familiar cosiness.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge the bakers’ work.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: For the first time, viewers rather than the judges set the challenges on The Great British Bake Off. The episode asked contestants to make cheesecake with a family member, different bakes for the technical and an edible wearable showstopper.

segments.title: A little more bite
segments.body: The review argues that the week’s novelty mattered even though the results were not especially chaotic. It also points to a more openly sparring relationship between Lawson and Hollywood, and less automatic sympathy for bakers when things go wrong, as signs that the series may be willing to loosen its carefully cosy format.

content.headline: Amy Dowden’s early Strictly exit raises questions about the show’s partnerships
content.shortHeadline: Amy Dowden’s Strictly exit exposes the stakes of pairing
content.standfirst: The review argues that Strictly’s professional dancers, not celebrity name recognition, often drive the audience’s investment. Amy Dowden’s second consecutive early exit prompts questions about how the show matches its couples and recognises its pros.

image.caption: Strictly professional dancer Amy Dowden.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Dowden’s exit exposes one big Strictly problem

segments.body: Amy Dowden was the first professional dancer eliminated from this year’s Strictly Come Dancing, for the second season in a row. The i Paper critic argues the result feels particularly unfair after a run of difficult seasons that included illness, injury and a controversial celebrity pairing.

segments.title: The partnerships are the point
segments.body: The review’s broader case is that professional dancers shape the relationships viewers follow and the way celebrity contestants develop on the show. It questions why Dowden was paired with a less experienced dancer when, in the critic’s view, her popularity and skill deserved a partner with a stronger chance of staying in the competition.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future off screen
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and has no announced next Doctor. Interviews with fans and writers trace the series’ changing fortunes but leave its return date—and its next creative direction—unknown.

image.caption: Several of Doctor Who’s incarnations, from Christopher Eccleston to Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since Ncuti Gatwa’s Doctor departed at the end of the 2025 series, the BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special. The corporation is seeking a new production partner, but none had stepped forward at the time of the report.

segments.title: A show built on renewal
segments.body: The article traces Doctor Who’s earlier cancellation in 1989 and revival in 2005, as well as the successive actors and showrunners who reshaped it. Fans and former contributors disagree on what went wrong in its latest era, citing questions about scripts, casting and the show’s use of a major streaming partner.

segments.title: What remains unsettled
segments.body: Interviewees insist the programme’s core values and appeal can survive another break, but the next Doctor, funding and production plans are not settled. The article captures a passionate audience’s worry that a long-running series could become an archive rather than return to broadcast television.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a new legal-drama spin-off
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up moves its family-law drama to Manchester
content.standfirst: The new series follows a Manchester firm led by Ritu Arya and Sanjeev Bhaskar, with a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its makers aim to keep the original’s family melodrama while giving a new group of writers room to shape it.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up returns to the family-law world of The Split, but moves its focus to Manchester and the Kishan family’s firm. Ritu Arya plays barrister Aria, whose plans to take over from her father are unsettled by grief, a former partner’s arrival and changes to the firm’s succession.

segments.title: Representation as everyday life
segments.body: The series has a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to portray a family living ordinary lives, rather than asking its characters to represent every aspect of a culture; Abi Morgan says the spin-off keeps the original’s focus on family conflict while supporting a new writing team.

content.headline: The £350 GTA VI collector’s box shows how gaming is pricing up
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s £350 collector’s box reflects gaming’s rising costs
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s merchandise bundle does not include the game, which costs extra. The Guardian’s games writer argues that the price reflects a widening divide between free-to-play mobile gaming and the console and PC titles increasingly treated as luxury purchases.

image.caption: Merchandise from Grand Theft Auto VI’s Vice City Collection.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection costs £350 and contains merchandise rather than the game itself. With the game priced separately at £70, buyers wanting both face a £420 bill.

segments.title: A market divided
segments.body: The writer says expensive special editions have become more common, alongside rising console and game costs. Citing Newzoo’s estimate that around 80% of players use free or low-cost mobile games, the article argues that the premium market is increasingly aimed at the smaller group able to spend more on consoles, games and collectibles.

The piece distinguishes the broad accessibility of phone games from the console and PC experiences the writer values. As physical games become harder to find, those larger-scale titles may become more difficult to buy second-hand as well as more expensive at launch.

content.headline: Silver Pines review: a stylish detective game built from noir’s ruins
content.shortHeadline: Silver Pines is a moody, rewarding neo-noir detective game
content.standfirst: This 2D adventure follows a private eye searching for a missing musician through a deserted town of payphones, clues and monsters. The review finds familiar mechanics elevated by meticulous atmosphere, deliberate pacing and a carefully built mythology.

image.caption: A rain-darkened street in Silver Pines.

sources.originalTitle: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

segments.body: In Silver Pines, private investigator Red Walker searches a deserted town for a missing singer-songwriter. Players explore abandoned shops, apartments and sewers, collecting clues and solving puzzles while the mystery deepens and survival-horror threats emerge.

segments.title: Style as an invitation to explore
segments.body: The review says the game’s point-and-click and Metroidvania elements are familiar, but its visual design is unusually assured. Rotoscoped animation, layered scenery, careful lighting and a sleazy jazz soundtrack establish a noir world that rewards slow exploration.

Combat is tense and the puzzles can be opaque, though the difficulty can be lowered for players more interested in the story. The reviewer relishes the game’s references to films and television including Blue Velvet, Twin Peaks and The X-Files, and its invitation to wander rather than rush.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has thrilling combat but little else to sustain it
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s combat shines in a repetitive prequel
content.standfirst: The prequel returns to the alien invasion that defined the series, with the strongest combat in years. The review says repetitive routes, excessive collectibles and limited changes to the story leave the campaign feeling padded.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day revisits the opening of the Locust invasion, putting players alongside Marcus Fenix and three other soldiers as creatures emerge from beneath the ground. Its early hours recapture some of the horror and tactical cover-based action associated with the first Gears of War games.

segments.title: A campaign that circles back
segments.body: The review finds the combat excellent: movement is more fluid, weapons feel powerful and destruction makes firefights dynamic. But the campaign repeatedly sends players across the same parts of the city, adds large areas of collectibles and side activities, and offers few meaningful changes to the pace.

The critic argues that E-Day’s strongest horror sequences occupy too little of the game, while some collectibles even interrupt emotional scenes. The result is an entertaining combat system inside a safe, repetitive prequel that rarely builds on its early ideas.

content.headline: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil adapts the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil finds its horror in the experience of play
content.standfirst: Rather than centre familiar heroes, the film follows an ordinary courier through a world of scarce ammunition, cryptic clues and escalating danger. The Guardian argues that this makes it one of the more interesting adaptations of a game series.

image.caption: Zach Cregger and Austin Abrams on the set of Resident Evil.
